query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐solidified, Co‑free FeNiCrMn, there exists a critical defect accumulation threshold – defined by a rapid increase in the density of dislocations, stacking faults, and twins – that triggers a transition from primarily dislocation‐mediated plasticity to a twin‐dominated and locally incipient amorphization regime. This transition, which is sensitive to both strain rate and temperature, is responsible for the enhanced strain hardening and maintained strength–ductility balance observed under dynamic loading.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐solidified, single‐phase Co‑free FeNiCrMn alloy with minimal prior deformation and a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled dynamic compression experiments using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar system over a matrix of strain rates (e.g., 900 s⁻¹ to 4600 s⁻¹) and temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, ambient, and moderately elevated temperatures).
generation.conditions: Dynamic loading under varying strain rates and temperatures while maintaining a Co‑free composition; experiments should be conducted on as‐solidified material to avoid effects from prior recrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid accumulation of crystalline defects – specifically dislocations, stacking faults, and twin boundaries – that, once surpassing a critical threshold, mediate a shift in the dominant deformation mechanism.
generation.mechanism: Under increasing strain rate or at lower temperatures, the defect accumulation in the FeNiCrMn alloy reaches a critical density at which dislocation slip is hindered and twinning (with localized proto‐amorphous regions along deformation bands) is activated. This mechanistic transition enhances strain hardening and dynamic strengthening, thereby preserving the balance between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Experiments will show that, above a well-defined combination of strain rate and temperature, there is an abrupt increase in twin density (and possibly traces of amorphous regions) that correlates with a jump in yield strength and work hardening rate as revealed by stress–strain curves. In situ and post-mortem microstructural analyses (using high-resolution SEM/TEM and digital image correlation) will register this threshold behavior.
generation.baseline: Quasi-static loading at ambient temperature where deformation is predominantly governed by homogeneous dislocation motion with lower strain hardening and no distinctly enhanced twin formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to as‐solidified Co‑free FeNiCrMn with a uniform initial microstructure; at very extreme temperatures or if significant secondary phase precipitation occurs from additional processing, other mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the defect‐accumulation threshold concept observed in Co‑containing HEAs (e.g., as discussed in PMC7846165::web::012::results_and_discussion and PMC7512474::web::016::5_conclusions) to a Co‑free system. It is uncertain whether the exact defect density threshold and the degree of twin versus amorphous zone formation will directly mirror prior observations given likely differences in stacking-fault energies and initial defect states.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a suite of dynamic compression tests on as‐solidified FeNiCrMn specimens across a defined matrix of strain rates and temperatures. Use in situ high-speed SEM (or TEM) with digital image correlation to quantify real-time defect formation (dislocation density, twin fraction, and any amorphous features) coupled with full-field stress–strain measurements.
measurements: Stress–strain behavior (yield strength, work hardening rate, serration characteristics) at each test condition
Quantitative microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM imaging and DIC) to measure the density of dislocations, stacking faults, and twin boundaries immediately after dynamic loading
Correlation of measured defect densities with changes in mechanical response
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no distinct threshold in defect density (i.e., a sudden increase in twin and/or amorphous regions) is observed when transitioning from quasi-static to dynamic regimes, or if the changes in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and strain hardening) vary continuously with strain rate and temperature without any correlated microstructural transition, then the hypothesis that a critical defect accumulation threshold governs the dynamic behavior is falsified.

Serration characteristics are ubiquitous in many structural and functional materials such as high-entropy alloy (AlCoCr1.5Fe1.5NiTi0.5, Al0.3CoCrFeNi etc.). It would lead to the instability of mechanical properties. By studying the serration behavior, it may be possible to have an early warning signal for oncoming epileptic seizures and perhaps economic trends. In the present work, we used the split-Hopkinson pressure bar to investigate the dynamic mechanical behavior of NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy prepared by arc melting. The aims are: (1) To report the mechanical properties and microstructure under dynamic loadings, (2) to obtain the plastic model, and (3) to discuss the microstructural mechanism for the serration behavior when the alloy deforms at high strain rates.

The as-cast equiatomic NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy has a simple FCC crystallographic structure. Serration behavior is observed in the stress- strain curves of the as-cast NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed at dynamic loadings. The yield strength of the high-entropy alloy, which distributes from 490 to 800 MPa, presents a positive relationship with the strain rates. The Johnson–Cook plastic model and the Zerilli–Armstrong plastic model of the NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy are obtained. However, the results predicted by Zerilli–Armstrong correspond better with the experimental results. The serration behavior of the NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy at a high strain rate is sensitive to the strain rates. The high density of deformation bands plays an important role in the deformation behavior and mechanical properties of the as-cast NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed at dynamic loadings.

Thus, we conclude that extreme plastic deformation, achieved by dynamic loading, is sufficient to induce the fcc→hcp transition. The same energetic argument can be used to explain the amorphization as the amorphous phase is energetically less favorable at ambient conditions. Upon severe plastic deformation, when a higher critical defect concentration is reached, the hcp structure and the heavily deformed fcc matrix can transform, via a solid-state process, to an amorphous phase. Nevertheless, one can envisage the broader scenario shown in schematic fashion in Fig. 4. Specifically, as the deformation energy, and accordingly the defect density, is increased, elastic deformation gives way to the generation of dislocations and their motion, then to deformation twinning, then phase transitions until finally in the extreme high strain (and/or high strain rate) regime, where amorphization can occur. The boundary between each mechanism can be loosely delineated by critical defect densities, which shift the free-energy barrier between different phases. The CrMnFeCoNi HEA has a very low stacking-fault energy, which favors defect accumulation during deformation since low stacking-fault energies lead to the dissociation of dislocations with a larger spacing between the partials; this, in turn, acts to severely inhibit the cross-slip of screw dislocations and consequently reduces the probability of dislocation annihilation.
